# Generalized Sum with Countable Non-zero Summands — Corollary

## 0. The statement, its two ambiguities, and what will be proved

**Setting.** Let $V$ be a Banach space (over $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$) with norm $\|\cdot\|$. Let $(v_i)_{i\in I}$ be an indexed family of elements of $V$, and put
$$S:=\{\,i\in I: v_i\ne 0\,\}\qquad(\text{the \emph{support} of the family}).$$
Let $J,K\subseteq I$ be countably infinite subsets with $S\subseteq J\cap K$, let $(j_n)$ be a countably infinite enumeration of $J$ and $(k_n)$ one of $K$ (i.e. bijections from a set of consecutive natural numbers onto $J$, resp. onto $K$), and let $r\in\mathbb{R}_{>0}$.

**Assertion to be examined.**
$$\sum_{n} v_{j_n}\ \text{converges absolutely to } r \iff \sum_{n} v_{k_n}\ \text{converges absolutely to } r .$$

Two points of the formulation have to be pinned down first.

### 0.1 What "converges absolutely to $r$" means

A series $\sum_n w_n$ in a normed space *converges absolutely* iff the real series $\sum_n\|w_n\|$ converges. Since $r$ is a **positive real number** while the $v_i$ are vectors of an arbitrary Banach space $V$, the only reading that is type-correct in this generality is

> **(A)** $\ \sum_n\|v_{j_n}\|$ converges and $\sum_n\|v_{j_n}\|=r$.

This is the reading under which we prove the corollary. For completeness we also handle

> **(B)** $\ \sum_n\|v_{j_n}\|$ converges **and** $\sum_n v_{j_n}=r$, where $r$ is read as an element of $V$ (meaningful e.g. when $V=\mathbb{R}$),

by proving (Theorem 2) that under absolute convergence the two *vector* sums coincide. So the corollary is established under either reading, and nothing in what follows depends on which one is intended.

### 0.2 The range of the summation index: the statement as literally written is false

The statement displays the enumerations as $\{j_0,j_1,j_2,\ldots\}$ and $\{k_0,k_1,k_2,\ldots\}$, indexed from $0$, but displays the series as $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}$. Read literally — enumerations indexed from $0$, series beginning at $n=1$ — the assertion is **false**: the two series then silently discard the terms $v_{j_0}$ and $v_{k_0}$, which need not be equal, or even both zero.

> **Counterexample to the literal reading.** Take $V=\mathbb{R}$ (a Banach space), $I=\mathbb{N}=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$, and
> $$v_0=1,\qquad v_1=2,\qquad v_i=0\ \ (i\ge2).$$
> Then $S=\{0,1\}$. Take $J=K=\mathbb{N}$; these are countably infinite and $S\subseteq J\cap K=\mathbb{N}$. Enumerate
> $$j_n=n\quad(n\ge0);\qquad k_0=1,\ \ k_1=0,\ \ k_n=n\ \ (n\ge2).$$
> Both $n\mapsto j_n$ and $n\mapsto k_n$ are bijections $\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}$, hence legitimate countably infinite enumerations of $J$ and of $K$. Now
> $$\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\|v_{j_n}\|=\|v_1\|+\|v_2\|+\cdots=2+0+0+\cdots=2,$$
> $$\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\|v_{k_n}\|=\|v_{k_1}\|+\|v_{k_2}\|+\cdots=\|v_0\|+0+0+\cdots=1 .$$
> With $r=2\in\mathbb{R}_{>0}$: the first series converges absolutely to $r$, the second does not (it converges absolutely to $1\ne 2$). The same witness refutes reading (B), since $\sum_{n=1}^\infty v_{j_n}=2$ while $\sum_{n=1}^\infty v_{k_n}=1$.

This is a typographical off-by-one, not the mathematical content: the intended hypothesis is that **each series runs over the entire enumeration of its index set**. (It is an instance of a general trap: if one enumerates a set from index $0$ but sums from index $1$, one is summing over $J\setminus\{j_0\}$, not over $J$, and no theorem about $J$ can be expected to survive.) The repair is to align the two conventions, in either of the two equivalent ways:

* index the enumerations from $1$, $J=\{j_1,j_2,j_3,\ldots\}$ and $K=\{k_1,k_2,k_3,\ldots\}$, and keep the series $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}$; **or**
* keep the enumerations indexed from $0$ and take the series to be $\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}$.

Accordingly we fix once and for all a set of consecutive natural numbers
$$\mathcal{N}\in\bigl\{\{0,1,2,\ldots\},\ \{1,2,3,\ldots\}\bigr\},$$
**the same $\mathcal{N}$ for both enumerations**, let $\varphi:\mathcal{N}\to J$, $\varphi(n)=j_n$, and $\psi:\mathcal{N}\to K$, $\psi(n)=k_n$, be bijections, and write $\sum_{n\in\mathcal{N}}$ for the corresponding series $\lim_{N\to\infty}\sum_{n\in\mathcal{N},\,n\le N}$. Every argument below is verbatim the same for the two choices of $\mathcal{N}$; indeed the two index sets are order-isomorphic, so both repaired versions are proved at once. This is the **corrected corollary**, and it is true:

> **Corrected Corollary.** With the setting above and $r\in\mathbb{R}_{>0}$:
> $$\sum_{n\in\mathcal{N}} v_{j_n}\ \text{converges absolutely to } r\iff \sum_{n\in\mathcal{N}} v_{k_n}\ \text{converges absolutely to } r .$$

It follows from Theorems 1 and 2 below, which are proved in §2–§3.

### 0.3 A caveat about "rearrangement"

The result must **not** be argued by "addition is commutative, so the order of summation is irrelevant": for series that converge only conditionally the sum genuinely depends on the order (Riemann's rearrangement theorem: the alternating harmonic series $1-\tfrac12+\tfrac13-\cdots=\ln 2$ can be rearranged to sum to any prescribed real number). What makes the present statement work is that the series being compared are series of the **non-negative** reals $\|v_{j_n}\|$, for which order-independence is a theorem (Lemma 1 below), and that the *vector* series are assumed **absolutely** convergent, which is precisely the hypothesis under which rearrangement is harmless. Both facts are proved from scratch below; no unjustified commutation of infinite sums is used.

---

## 1. Conventions and two lemmas

For a **finite** set $E$ and real numbers $(a_i)_{i\in E}$, the symbol $\sum_{i\in E}a_i$ denotes the ordinary finite sum, which is well defined independently of the order in which the terms are added, by the generalized commutative and associative laws for addition in $\mathbb{R}$ (proved by induction on $|E|$); the same applies to finite sums of vectors in $V$, using commutativity and associativity of vector addition. For $E=\varnothing$ the sum is $0$ (resp. $0_V$). If $E=F\sqcup G$ is a disjoint decomposition then $\sum_{i\in E}a_i=\sum_{i\in F}a_i+\sum_{i\in G}a_i$; and if $\theta:F\to E$ is a bijection then $\sum_{n\in F}a_{\theta(n)}=\sum_{i\in E}a_i$ (finite reindexing). These are the only "rearrangement" facts used, and they concern finite sums only.

For $A\subseteq I$ define the **finite-subsum supremum**
$$\Sigma_A:=\sup\Bigl\{\ \sum_{i\in E}\|v_i\|\ :\ E\subseteq A,\ E\text{ finite}\ \Bigr\}\ \in\ [0,+\infty],$$
the supremum taken in the extended reals. The set on the right is non-empty (it contains the value $0$, attained at $E=\varnothing$), so $\Sigma_A\ge0$ always, including for $A=\varnothing$, where $\Sigma_\varnothing=0$.

### Lemma 1 (a non-negative series equals the supremum of its finite subsums)

Let $\mathcal{N}$ be as in §0.2 and let $(a_n)_{n\in\mathcal{N}}$ be non-negative real numbers. For $N\in\mathcal{N}$ put $s_N:=\sum_{n\in\mathcal{N},\,n\le N}a_n$, and put
$$\sigma:=\sup\Bigl\{\ \sum_{n\in F}a_n\ :\ F\subseteq\mathcal{N},\ F\text{ finite}\ \Bigr\}\in[0,+\infty].$$
Then:

1. $\sup_{N\in\mathcal{N}}s_N=\sigma$ (as elements of $[0,+\infty]$);
2. $\sum_{n\in\mathcal{N}}a_n$ converges if and only if $\sigma<+\infty$, and in that case $\sum_{n\in\mathcal{N}}a_n=\sigma$; if $\sigma=+\infty$ the series diverges (its partial sums tend to $+\infty$).

*Proof.* (1) "$\le$": each partial sum is itself a finite subsum, $s_N=\sum_{n\in F_N}a_n$ with $F_N:=\{n\in\mathcal{N}: n\le N\}$ finite; hence $s_N\le\sigma$ for every $N$, and so $\sup_N s_N\le\sigma$.

"$\ge$": let $F\subseteq\mathcal{N}$ be finite. If $F=\varnothing$, then $\sum_{n\in F}a_n=0\le s_{N_0}$ where $N_0=\min\mathcal{N}$, because $s_{N_0}=a_{N_0}\ge0$. If $F\ne\varnothing$, put $N:=\max F\in\mathcal{N}$; then $F\subseteq F_N$ and, by the disjoint-decomposition rule $F_N=F\sqcup(F_N\setminus F)$,
$$s_N-\sum_{n\in F}a_n=\sum_{n\in F_N\setminus F}a_n\ \ge\ 0 ,$$
since every $a_n\ge0$ (a finite sum of non-negative reals is non-negative). Hence $\sum_{n\in F}a_n\le s_N\le\sup_N s_N$. Taking the supremum over all finite $F\subseteq\mathcal{N}$ gives $\sigma\le\sup_N s_N$. Together, $\sup_N s_N=\sigma$.

(2) Enumerate $\mathcal{N}=\{N_0<N_1<N_2<\cdots\}$; then $s_{N_{m+1}}-s_{N_m}=a_{N_{m+1}}\ge0$, so the sequence of partial sums is non-decreasing. By the monotone convergence theorem for real sequences (a direct consequence of the least-upper-bound property of $\mathbb{R}$), a non-decreasing real sequence converges iff it is bounded above, and then its limit equals its supremum; if it is unbounded above it diverges to $+\infty$. By (1) the partial sums are bounded above iff $\sigma<+\infty$, and then $\sum_{n\in\mathcal{N}}a_n=\lim_m s_{N_m}=\sup_N s_N=\sigma$. $\blacksquare$

Note that $\sigma$ is defined purely in terms of the *set* of values $\{a_n\}$ together with their multiplicities and involves no ordering of $\mathcal{N}$; this is the precise sense in which a non-negative series is order-independent, and it is the engine of the whole proof.

### Lemma 2 (the finite-subsum supremum sees only the support)

Let $A\subseteq I$ with $S\subseteq A$, where $S=\{i\in I:v_i\ne0\}$. Then $\Sigma_A=\Sigma_S$.

*Proof.* Since $S\subseteq A$, every finite subset of $S$ is also a finite subset of $A$, so the set of numbers whose supremum defines $\Sigma_A$ contains the set defining $\Sigma_S$; hence $\Sigma_S\le\Sigma_A$.

Conversely, let $E\subseteq A$ be finite. Splitting $E=(E\cap S)\sqcup(E\setminus S)$ and noting that $i\notin S$ implies $v_i=0$, hence $\|v_i\|=0$, we get
$$\sum_{i\in E}\|v_i\|=\sum_{i\in E\cap S}\|v_i\|+\sum_{i\in E\setminus S}\|v_i\|=\sum_{i\in E\cap S}\|v_i\|+0=\sum_{i\in E\cap S}\|v_i\| .$$
Since $E\cap S$ is a finite subset of $S$, this is $\le\Sigma_S$. Taking the supremum over all finite $E\subseteq A$ yields $\Sigma_A\le\Sigma_S$. Hence $\Sigma_A=\Sigma_S$. $\blacksquare$

(The degenerate cases are covered: if $S=\varnothing$ then every finite subsum over $A$ is $0$ and $\Sigma_A=0=\Sigma_S$; the empty set is allowed as an $E$ throughout.)

---

## 2. Theorem 1: the two series of norms have the same value

### Theorem 1

In the setting of §0 with the convention of §0.2 ($\mathcal{N}$ fixed, $\varphi:\mathcal{N}\to J$ and $\psi:\mathcal{N}\to K$ bijections), we have the identity in $[0,+\infty]$
$$\sum_{n\in\mathcal{N}}\|v_{j_n}\|\;=\;\Sigma_S\;=\;\sum_{n\in\mathcal{N}}\|v_{k_n}\|,$$
where a divergent series of non-negative terms is given the value $+\infty$. Consequently, for **every** $r\in\mathbb{R}$ (in particular every $r\in\mathbb{R}_{>0}$):
$$\Bigl(\textstyle\sum_{n\in\mathcal{N}}\|v_{j_n}\|\ \text{converges with sum } r\Bigr)\iff\Bigl(\textstyle\sum_{n\in\mathcal{N}}\|v_{k_n}\|\ \text{converges with sum } r\Bigr).$$

*Proof.* Set $a_n:=\|v_{j_n}\|\ge0$ for $n\in\mathcal{N}$. By Lemma 1,
$$\sum_{n\in\mathcal{N}}\|v_{j_n}\|=\sigma_J:=\sup\Bigl\{\sum_{n\in F}\|v_{j_n}\|\ :\ F\subseteq\mathcal{N}\text{ finite}\Bigr\}\in[0,+\infty],$$
the left-hand side being $+\infty$ exactly when the series diverges.

**Step 1: $\sigma_J=\Sigma_J$.** The map $F\mapsto\varphi(F)$ sends finite subsets of $\mathcal{N}$ to finite subsets of $J$ (the image of a finite set is finite), and it is a bijection onto the collection of finite subsets of $J$: its inverse is $E\mapsto\varphi^{-1}(E)$, which is finite because $\varphi$ is injective (so $|\varphi^{-1}(E)|=|E|$), and $\varphi(\varphi^{-1}(E))=E$ since $\varphi$ is surjective onto $J$, while $\varphi^{-1}(\varphi(F))=F$ since $\varphi$ is injective. Moreover, for each finite $F\subseteq\mathcal{N}$ the restriction $\varphi|_F:F\to\varphi(F)$ is a bijection, so finite reindexing gives
$$\sum_{n\in F}\|v_{j_n}\|=\sum_{n\in F}\|v_{\varphi(n)}\|=\sum_{i\in\varphi(F)}\|v_i\| .$$
Hence the two sets of real numbers
$$\Bigl\{\sum_{n\in F}\|v_{j_n}\|: F\subseteq\mathcal{N}\text{ finite}\Bigr\}\quad\text{and}\quad\Bigl\{\sum_{i\in E}\|v_i\|: E\subseteq J\text{ finite}\Bigr\}$$
are *equal*, and therefore have the same supremum: $\sigma_J=\Sigma_J$.

**Step 2: $\Sigma_J=\Sigma_S=\Sigma_K$.** By hypothesis $S\subseteq J\cap K$, so $S\subseteq J$ and $S\subseteq K$. Lemma 2 applied with $A=J$ and with $A=K$ gives $\Sigma_J=\Sigma_S$ and $\Sigma_K=\Sigma_S$.

**Step 3.** Steps 1 and 2 give $\sum_{n\in\mathcal{N}}\|v_{j_n}\|=\Sigma_S$. Running Steps 1–2 verbatim with $\psi$, $K$, $k_n$ in place of $\varphi$, $J$, $j_n$ gives $\sum_{n\in\mathcal{N}}\|v_{k_n}\|=\Sigma_K=\Sigma_S$. This is the asserted identity.

Finally, for $r\in\mathbb{R}$: by Lemma 1(2), "$\sum_{n\in\mathcal{N}}\|v_{j_n}\|$ converges with sum $r$" holds iff $\Sigma_S<+\infty$ and $\Sigma_S=r$, i.e. iff the element $\Sigma_S\in[0,+\infty]$ equals the real number $r$. The corresponding statement for $K$ is, by the same identity, a statement about the *same* quantity $\Sigma_S$ and $r$. Hence the two statements are equivalent. $\blacksquare$

**Remark.** Theorem 1 uses neither the completeness of $V$ nor the hypothesis $r>0$: it is valid in any normed vector space and for every real $r$. (For $r\le0$ both sides are simply false, since $\Sigma_S\ge0$ and $\Sigma_S=0$ would force $r=0$; the hypothesis $r>0$ is harmless but unnecessary.) Completeness enters only in Theorem 2.

---

## 3. Theorem 2: under absolute convergence the vector sums agree

### Theorem 2

Assume, in addition to the setting of §0/§0.2, that $\Sigma_S<+\infty$ (equivalently, by Theorem 1, that either — hence each — of the two series of norms converges). Then both series $\sum_{n\in\mathcal{N}}v_{j_n}$ and $\sum_{n\in\mathcal{N}}v_{k_n}$ converge in $V$, and
$$\sum_{n\in\mathcal{N}}v_{j_n}=\sum_{n\in\mathcal{N}}v_{k_n} .$$

*Proof.* Write $\mathcal{N}=\{N_0<N_1<\cdots\}$ and $x_M:=\sum_{n\in\mathcal{N},\,n\le N_M}v_{j_n}$ for the $M$-th partial sum.

**Convergence.** For $M'>M$, the triangle inequality (applied finitely often) gives
$$\|x_{M'}-x_M\|=\Bigl\|\sum_{m=M+1}^{M'}v_{j_{N_m}}\Bigr\|\ \le\ \sum_{m=M+1}^{M'}\|v_{j_{N_m}}\| .$$
By Theorem 1 the real series $\sum_{n\in\mathcal{N}}\|v_{j_n}\|$ converges, so its partial sums form a Cauchy sequence; thus, given $\varepsilon>0$ there is $M_\varepsilon$ with $\sum_{m=M+1}^{M'}\|v_{j_{N_m}}\|<\varepsilon$ whenever $M'>M\ge M_\varepsilon$. Hence $(x_M)_{M\ge0}$ is a Cauchy sequence in $V$; since $V$ is a Banach space, it converges. Write $x:=\sum_{n\in\mathcal{N}}v_{j_n}=\lim_M x_M\in V$. The same argument applied to $\psi$ gives $y:=\sum_{n\in\mathcal{N}}v_{k_n}\in V$.

**Equality.** Let $\varepsilon>0$. Since $\Sigma_S=\sup\bigl\{\sum_{i\in E}\|v_i\|: E\subseteq S\text{ finite}\bigr\}$ is a finite real number, by the approximation property of the supremum there is a finite set $E_0\subseteq S$ with
$$\sum_{i\in E_0}\|v_i\|>\Sigma_S-\varepsilon. \tag{$*$}$$

*Sub-claim.* For every finite $E$ with $E_0\subseteq E\subseteq J$ we have $\sum_{i\in E\setminus E_0}\|v_i\|<\varepsilon$.
Indeed, $E$ is a finite subset of $J$, so $\sum_{i\in E}\|v_i\|\le\Sigma_J=\Sigma_S$ (Theorem 1, Step 2), and by the disjoint decomposition $E=E_0\sqcup(E\setminus E_0)$ together with $(*)$,
$$\sum_{i\in E\setminus E_0}\|v_i\|=\sum_{i\in E}\|v_i\|-\sum_{i\in E_0}\|v_i\|<\Sigma_S-(\Sigma_S-\varepsilon)=\varepsilon. \tag{$**$}$$

Now, $E_0\subseteq S\subseteq J$ and $E_0$ is finite, so $\varphi^{-1}(E_0)\subseteq\mathcal{N}$ is finite; choose $M_0$ so large that $\varphi^{-1}(E_0)\subseteq\{N_0,\ldots,N_{M_0}\}$ (take $M_0=0$ if $E_0=\varnothing$). For $M\ge M_0$ set $E_M:=\{j_n: n\in\mathcal{N},\ n\le N_M\}=\varphi(\{N_0,\dots,N_M\})$; then $E_0\subseteq E_M\subseteq J$, $E_M$ is finite, and since $\varphi$ is injective the finite reindexing rule gives $x_M=\sum_{i\in E_M}v_i$. Therefore, by the triangle inequality and $(**)$ applied to $E=E_M$,
$$\Bigl\|x_M-\sum_{i\in E_0}v_i\Bigr\|=\Bigl\|\sum_{i\in E_M\setminus E_0}v_i\Bigr\|\le\sum_{i\in E_M\setminus E_0}\|v_i\|<\varepsilon\qquad(M\ge M_0).$$
Letting $M\to\infty$ and using continuity of the norm (which follows from $\bigl|\|u\|-\|w\|\bigr|\le\|u-w\|$),
$$\Bigl\|x-\sum_{i\in E_0}v_i\Bigr\|\le\varepsilon .$$

The set $E_0$ was chosen inside $S$, and $S\subseteq K$ as well; also $\Sigma_K=\Sigma_S$. Hence the sub-claim and the entire displayed argument hold verbatim with $K,\psi,k_n,y$ in place of $J,\varphi,j_n,x$, using the *same* $E_0$, and yield
$$\Bigl\|y-\sum_{i\in E_0}v_i\Bigr\|\le\varepsilon .$$

By the triangle inequality, $\|x-y\|\le\bigl\|x-\sum_{i\in E_0}v_i\bigr\|+\bigl\|\sum_{i\in E_0}v_i-y\bigr\|\le2\varepsilon$. Since $\varepsilon>0$ was arbitrary, $\|x-y\|=0$, hence $x=y$ by the positive-definiteness of the norm. $\blacksquare$

---

## 4. Proof of the corrected corollary

Let $V$, $(v_i)_{i\in I}$, $S$, $J$, $K$, the enumerations $\varphi,\psi$ over the common index set $\mathcal{N}$, and $r\in\mathbb{R}_{>0}$ be as in §0/§0.2.

**Under reading (A).** "$\sum_{n\in\mathcal{N}}v_{j_n}$ converges absolutely to $r$" means $\sum_{n\in\mathcal{N}}\|v_{j_n}\|$ converges with sum $r$. By Theorem 1 this holds iff $\Sigma_S=r$, and likewise "$\sum_{n\in\mathcal{N}}v_{k_n}$ converges absolutely to $r$" holds iff $\Sigma_S=r$. The two conditions are therefore literally the same condition, so each implies the other. $\square$

**Under reading (B).** Suppose $\sum_{n\in\mathcal{N}}v_{j_n}$ converges absolutely with sum $r\in V$. Absolute convergence means $\sum_{n\in\mathcal{N}}\|v_{j_n}\|<\infty$, i.e. $\Sigma_S<\infty$ by Theorem 1; hence, again by Theorem 1, $\sum_{n\in\mathcal{N}}\|v_{k_n}\|=\Sigma_S<\infty$, so $\sum_{n\in\mathcal{N}}v_{k_n}$ converges absolutely as well, and by Theorem 2 its sum equals $\sum_{n\in\mathcal{N}}v_{j_n}=r$. Thus $\sum_{n\in\mathcal{N}}v_{k_n}$ converges absolutely to $r$. The converse implication is the same argument with the roles of $J$ and $K$ interchanged (the hypotheses are symmetric in $J$ and $K$). $\square$

In both readings:
$$\boxed{\ \sum_{n\in\mathcal{N}} v_{j_n}\ \text{converges absolutely to } r\iff \sum_{n\in\mathcal{N}} v_{k_n}\ \text{converges absolutely to } r\ }$$
which is the corollary, in its corrected (index-aligned) form. $\blacksquare$

---

## 5. Summary

* **What is true.** If $J$ and $K$ are countably infinite subsets of $I$ both containing the support $S=\{i:v_i\ne0\}$, then for *any* enumerations of $J$ and of $K$, the series of norms $\sum_n\|v_{j_n}\|$ and $\sum_n\|v_{k_n}\|$ have the *same* value in $[0,+\infty]$, namely $\Sigma_S=\sup\{\sum_{i\in E}\|v_i\| : E\subseteq S\text{ finite}\}$ — provided each series runs over the whole of its enumeration. Consequently one converges absolutely to $r$ iff the other does; and when they converge, the vector sums in the Banach space $V$ are equal too.
* **Why.** A series of non-negative reals equals the supremum of its finite subsums (Lemma 1), a quantity that does not refer to any ordering; finite subsums are unchanged by reindexing along a bijection and by discarding indices $i$ with $v_i=0$ (Lemma 2). Since $J$ and $K$ differ only by indices carrying the zero vector, they yield the same supremum. Completeness of $V$ then upgrades this to equality of the vector sums.
* **What is false.** The literal statement, with enumerations indexed from $0$ but series starting at $n=1$, fails: the counterexample of §0.2 ($V=\mathbb{R}$, $v_0=1$, $v_1=2$, $v_i=0$ for $i\ge2$, $J=K=\mathbb{N}$, $j_n=n$, $k_0=1$, $k_1=0$, $k_n=n$ for $n\ge2$, $r=2$) has $\sum_{n=1}^\infty\|v_{j_n}\|=2=r$ but $\sum_{n=1}^\infty\|v_{k_n}\|=1\ne r$. Aligning the index conventions (both from $0$, or both from $1$) removes the defect and gives the true statement proved above.
* **Hypotheses actually used.** Completeness of $V$ is needed only for the vector-sum statement (Theorem 2); the equivalence under reading (A) holds in any normed space. The hypothesis $r>0$ is not needed. The hypothesis $S\subseteq J\cap K$ is essential: it is exactly what makes both $\Sigma_J$ and $\Sigma_K$ collapse to $\Sigma_S$.
